title: Two Pharma Giants Who'd Never Met | Mankind & Dr. Reddy's | WTF is Pharma?

segments.text:
[narrator] India makes medicines that
heal billions of people across the world.
Most of them have no idea who's behind it.

After much demand, we brought together
two of India's pharma giants,

Dr Reddy's and Mankind, to help you,
the young entrepreneurs of this country,
grasp the industry's nuances.

Their products are household names,
probably consumed by you at some time,
and, of course, consumed by millions.

So we decided to put a face
to these stalwarts.

[Meghana] So, how do you talk yourself
into it everyday?

I suppose, to prove it to my family,
to my brother, that I'm worth something.
So, that was only one, but...

how can I make it to a level
that I can start respecting myself?

[Meghana] And I'm sure
you've been through multiple phases
of going through tough times.

Erm, the biggest challenge I ever had
was in our operations.

This happened in the mid-- last decade,
in the middle of the last decade, around.

We had safety incidents where, you know,
people died, and that really shook me up

and really put me in a deep state
of depression.
So, that was a very difficult time for me.

[narrator] Reddy Pharmaceuticals
is headed by G. V. Prasad

and brings in roughly three billion
in revenue.

Mankind is led by Rajeev Juneja
and his brother,

with an annual turnover
of about 40,000 crores.

With numbers like these, many would coast,
but not Rajeev or G.V.
Their hunger keeps pushing the boundaries.
Here's the thing nobody tells you.

India's called the pharmacy of the world,
but that's by volume.
By revenue, we're barely a rounding error.

We make the drugs,
but someone else makes the money.
So, who? And why?

And more importantly,
where does a 25-year-old
find an opening in all of this?
That's exactly what we asked.
What is the business opportunity here?

Can you guys think of anything else
for the 25-year-old?

There are 128 unicorns in India today,
there is one in pharma drug innovation.
[inaudible conversations]
So, this is very casual.

I was telling him earlier, Prasad,
our audience is largely young people

who want to start a business
in your industry.

So, we won't speak so much
about your company, in particular.

There's no controversy,
there's no underlying, kind of, stuff.

It's very much everything
a 25-year-old needs

to start a business
in the pharma industry.

So, think both of you
are professors today,

and you are teaching a class
of young 25-year-olds.

I am part of that class,
so I'll keep asking you questions.

Before we start, maybe you guys
can tell me a bit about yourself.

I know you guys already.
You're very successful, popular people.

But a little bit about your life
and how you got to be where you are.
Would you like to go first?

[Rajeev] I can go first.
I don't have any issues.

My name is Rajeev Juneja,
and I have one wife.
[laughter]

And I have five kids,
three daughters, two sons.

Daughters means,
I mean, they are daughter-in-laws,
and one granddaughter.
So, I come from a place called Meerut,
which is 60 kilometres away from Delhi.
I'm... I'm new in Delhi.
2004-2005, we came to Delhi.

And before that, my education,
my brought up, all was in Meerut.

And I'm a college dropout
because circumstances were like this.

And number one,
I was not interested in studies.

So that's why I got an excuse
that there's a compulsion in the family,
and the money is not there.

So, I used to go
to my brother's medical store.
There, I learned how to run a pharmacy.

Like people go to Grandma's place
in summer vacation,

I used to go to that medical store
for two months.

So, eight, nine months,
I worked over there.
That was from tenth class to PUC Part-1.

Then, one day, I said,
"I want to be a medical rep."

I became a medical rep
in my brother's company.
Worked ten years over there.
And there, I did a lot of things.

And started a company
called Mankind in 1995.

-It's been that long?
-Yeah, 30 years.
It's been a while.
One second. Don't hold him by the chain.
Don't... Leave him open.
I'm telling him don't keep the chain.
Okay, let's continue.
Today, whatever Mankind is,

is because of whatever,
I'll say, destiny dictates.

How did it go from pharmaceutical
to what it is now?

Like, your experience in working
in a pharmaceutical store
and starting Mankind, what worked?
See, what basically happens in life,

what you hate
becomes a big lesson for you.

I used to hate going to the pharmacy,
cleaning, sweeping...
buying goods from wholesale market...
at the age when my friends were enjoying.
So, that was the lesson.

How market really works,
how sales reps, how companies,

how doctors operate,
how this market operates.
I never knew that.

And then I became a medical rep
in a local kind of a company, it was.

Local means, in the sense,
a black-and-white company.

Not even colours were there
in boxes and visual aids or literatures.

So, when you work
in that kind of a company,
if you will not become a brand yourself,
company will not run,
where failure rate is 80%, 90%.
Every time just...

You become so thick-skinned,
at the same time, sensitive.
It was somewhat of an oxymoron.

Same time you are stubborn,
or thick-skinned,

at the same time,
you are very, very sensitive.

When you go through
that kind of a phase and...
these two enable that...
One time that company starts,

which was started
with 69,000 rupees in '84,
became Meerut's number-one company.

We had beaten Glaxo, Cipla,
any company, everybody, every company.

Sheer hard work, sheer hard work.
That's it.
I mean, we never gave up.

We have to do it any cost.
We didn't have any other choice.

When you have this kind of grit,
something good really happens.

We were almost
Western UP's top-ten companies.

And then,
some family separation was there.
So, me and my brother said,

"We'll start a new company,
and we've got 50 lakh rupees."

And in those days,
Bestochem was a ten-crore revenue company.

That's just a very peaceful partition,
and we wanted to get away.
Hmm.

[Rajeev] Every learning
was not in Mankind.

Every learning happened
during that time of huge struggle.
And what is Mankind today?

Can you explain that as well
for people who don't know?

[sighs] Mankind today is
the fourth-largest pharma company.
Uh...

The revenue of more than
40,000 crore rupees.

We are the company
which operates in veterinary side as well.
We operate in pet side as well.
We are a OTC company as well.
What's the biggest part?

-Of Mankind.
-The biggest part is pharma.
Biggest part, say, 85% is pharma.

What?
Is there one particular product in that?
Yeah.

One product, which is quite a big one,
is Telmikind.
It's for hypertension.

-Right.
-1,000 crore rupees.

-Right.
-Yeah.

Second brand would be Manforce.
That's quite a known name. Condoms.
Around, together, 600 crore rupees.
That is what Mankind is.

Mankind is basically...
People say it's a OTC kind of a company
because of Manforce.

But if you just look and go deeper down,
it's a pharma company.

Intentionally, we started OTC
because we wanted to be known.

When you start very small--
We started from Meerut,
and we are nothing.

And we never, ever started
all-India in one go.
First, Western UP only. First, made a try.

And slowly and gradually,
Eastern UP, then Haryana,
then Punjab, basically evolved.

Wherever we went, it's like
we were a small company rising very fast.

So, after all this,
what you basically see is respect, name.
And how can you get the name?
Then you come on television.
How can you come on television?
As a pharma company, you cannot come.
So, the launch happened.
[Nikhil] Hmm.

Your OTC company would be there.
In the end, your logo would be displayed.
Hmm.

And we used to keep logo
for a longer period.

Otherwise, just, generally,
it's half a second.
We used to keep it for more than a second.
That was the strategy.
Magazines, newspaper, every place.

So, actually, we basically wanted
to propagate Mankind all over India

before Mankind
is to be launched any place.
South side, we were not there.
We came to South 19 years back.
We are 30 years old.
But it was all gradual.
We were not in a hurry.
Our India was UP.

Our India became Haryana and Punjab,
and then UP.

-We never thought that India is one.
-Right.
All focused.
It was always very focused approach.
Deepest coverage.
And he's a scientist.
He's a different guy.

He comes from that top side
of the pyramid of pharma,

-R&D and other things.
-Right.

I always used to think
of you guys like commandos.

Come in, push forward all the competition
aside, and go ahead.
We basically call ourselves, I mean, FMCP.
FMCG of pharma.

-[Prasad] Hmm.
-[Rajeev] So, I mean...
We had nothing.

Same branded, generic
twenty brands were there.
No, but you are very unconventional.

-Yeah, totally.
-How you got into the market,
and how you pushed up.

Never followed anything
of the industry. Never.
Absolutely contrarian, 100%.

And even right now, if everybody
is doing something, I will not do it.
[Nikhil] Hmm.
If something is, then something's up.
What are you most bullish about today?
Is it "G" part of FMCG,
"P" part of FMCP, or the FMME?
[chuckles]

I'm most bullish now,
I mean, as you basically evolve,
we are going to come in his category.

-In which category?
-In his category.
These guys get very young R&D guys.

-That's our next goal.
-[Nikhil] Hmm.
Do you guys interact between yourselves?

-First time.
-I've never met him before.

-Never?
-Never.
Wow.

Should we go in and sit?
There's mosquito time in five--

-[Rajeev] Yeah, whatever you say.
-Fifteen minutes, there'll be mosquitoes.
[Prasad] It's sultry here.
But, I mean, if you just ask me,

mosquitoes in Delhi versus this place,
no mosquitoes.

-I can't see.
-No, they come, strangely,
at one particular time, at 5:45.

They suddenly come,
and then at 6:30, they are not there.

Yeah. Which is very strange.
I don't know where they come from.
But come, we can go inside.
What's up?
Chase.
Come.
Come.
Chase.
[indistinct conversations]
It saw the ball, sir, that's why.
[indistinct conversations continue]

[Meghana] So, for starters,
I wanted to understand,

what did your first day
in pharma look like?
Uh...

-Nervous. Bad. Very bad.
-[chuckling]
I ran away.

I... I mean, lied to my brother
that I worked,
because I had no confidence
in meeting, going in a medical college.

-That was the first reaction.
-Yeah.
[Meghana] What did your 1980s look like?

I was in college till '82, '83.
'82, '83 I was doing my master's,
decided not to study,

experienced
everything that life had to offer,
so, went to concerts, went to games,
that's how my '83 was.

I came back, joined my family business
which was in construction,

but, also, I started an entrepreneurial
venture in pharmaceuticals,

ran that for sometime,
it didn't do too well, then I exited.
[inaudible conversation]

[Meghana] And what is something in pharma
that you have seen from 1980s to now

that has changed
so significantly in India?

I think, you know,
when we started our business,

you just had to make the product
to make money.

Now we have to be very good,
excellent, highly competitive.

The business has become very crowded.
There are a lot many people here.
And the whole thing has scaled.
[inaudible conversation]

[Meghana] What was that day,
when you thought you have arrived?

-Maybe third year.
-Okay.
Third year. Three years.

[Meghana] And what do you think
changed that day?

I found a few mentors,
actually, to be very honest.
Uh...
I can call them mentors now.

In those days, they were my gurus,
or whatever you call it.

I made a choice that I should be
in the company of smart people.

[Meghana] And did something, you know,
significantly shift when you say,

"Okay, I have made it now,
and I don't need to be worried"?

What was that moment?
Like, did you buy something?

Did you have access to something
that you didn't have before?
What was that?
Till now, that day has not come.

-Honestly.
-[Meghana chuckles]
[inaudible conversation]
[Meghana] Have you always loved science?

-I always liked science. Yeah.
-Interesting.
I really loved it because it's like magic.

You take simple molecules,
combine them to make complex molecules.

-Suddenly, this molecule cures a disease.
-Yeah.

-And what made you come back?
-I was always...

-I never thought I'll settle in the US.
-Really?

I mean, that's so different for
so many people who grew up in that era.
I think business families generally

expected children to come back,
so I was kind of...

And what would your advice be for someone
who's growing up in a business family?

At the time, actually,
I wanted to do a PhD.

But I got admission,
but my father's business was...

He was going through some trouble
and asked me to come back and join him.

I'd ask people now to do
what they love to do, what their dream is.
[narrator] Fate has its own way.

Mr. G.V. Prasad came back to India to run
the family construction business.

He then went on to start his first
pharmaceutical venture with his father.

Their factory was right next to one
belonging to Dr Anji Reddy,
who was already a successful entrepreneur.

Around this time,
he got married to Dr. Anuradha Reddy,
who was Dr. Reddy's daughter.

In 1988, the new pharma venture
was not scaling,

and his father-in-law,
growing fast and needing capacity

for Dr. Reddy's Laboratories,
bought the plant and merged it with his.

G.V. Prasad moved on,
went back to construction,
and then, one day, the phone rang.

Dr. Reddy was running two companies
at the time, Cheminor Drugs
and Dr. Reddy's Laboratories.

The co-founder of Cheminor Drugs
had parted ways due to differences.
Dr. Reddy needed someone he could trust.
G.V. Prasad said yes without thinking.

That was 1990. He became
the CEO of Cheminor Drugs.
The group was doing under 100 crores.
He ran one company, built it, scaled it,

and in 2001,
Cheminor merged with Dr. Reddy's
and was listed on NYSE.

Before Dr. Anji Reddy passed,
he wrote a book.
He called it An Unfinished Agenda.

A dream of discovering new molecules,
new cures,
a truly Indian pharamceutical legacy.
He didn't live to see it completed.

The effort still continues through
Aurigene Oncology.
[inaudible conversations]

-We'll sit at the table so we get light?
-Yes, sir.

[Meghana] So, what would you say
is the one differentiating advice

that you would give to someone
who's building in this space?

-In pharma?
-Yeah.

I'd say be careful which part
of the business you're entering.

Enter a space
where there is room to play, grow,
and mistakes can be tolerated.

Focus on where your strength lies,
where your competitive advantage will be,

what problem that you're solving
in a unique way, and get into that.
Think through all this before you jump in.

[inaudible] But the most important thing
is, failures are part of life.

with establishing
the Indian pharma industry,

then we get into
the different molecules and...

-Yeah, okay.

So... let me start with

We'll focus on Rajeev more
for business and...

-Perfectly fine.
-...Professor Prasad more on science.
[Rajeev] Even I'm learning from him.
I mean, the certain things...

I mean, I keep talking to my R&D guy,
and he explains me things.

Then it really goes away because
my mind is always there somewhere else.

-Right.
-Actually, I'm not a scientist also.

See, I mean, somebody who has
spent so many years over there

in majorly science side,
I mean, you become knowledgeable.
Yeah, yeah.
For me, you're a scientist.

Yeah, so let me start
with the segmentation.
[Nikhil] Okay.

Broadly, the industry
has four or five verticals,
if you call them in IT language.
API, active ingredient.

[Nikhil] You want to start
by biggest vertical to smallest?

From an Indian context,
the biggest one is pharmaceuticals.

-Okay.
-Generic pharmaceuticals.

-Generic pharma is the biggest?
-Yeah. They're branded generics, actually.
It's the biggest vertical.

It's actually copies of products
which were discovered,

innovated by major pharmaceuticals
around the world.
We make them equivalent to them.

And there's a whole study on
how do you manage equivalence.
I don't know if you want to know that.

-So you explain how a drug is discovered.
-Yeah.

-Then you explain patent.
-Yeah.

So once the patent runs out,
then the generic starts?

Even before it runs out,
you can do the R&D work.

Keep it ready for the day

company decide which pharmaceutical
company in India, China,

whichever country do
they give the contract to?

They don't get anything.
They don't have a say on this.

Anybody who wants to do it
after the patent expires is free to do it.
So, it's like this.
The innovator discovers drugs.

He has a protected monopoly
for a few years.

-[Rajeev] 15 years.
-Once, yeah, it depends.
Once the patent runs out,

you can, anybody in the world can
develop an equivalent product.

with the health authorities
that it is really an equivalent product.

or you say semaglutide
discovered by Novo Nordisk.

because you just have
to establish, analytically,

that they are the same solution
that you are putting in the body.

Sometimes, they are not.
Then, you have to do studies on humans.

Tablets, you have to establish that
the release of the drug in your body

is equivalent to the way the innovator's
product is released in the body.

Right? When you take a pill,
it goes into your digestive tract,

it passes the thing
and it goes into your bloodstream,

cleanses it out of your system.

and the ingredient acts on the cells

that it needs to act
and cures your disease.
It's like a lock and key.

The protein is there
and your drug goes there

and corrects whatever needs
to be corrected.

So, there is a concentration
of the product in your blood.

When you take a tablet for the next
24 hours, 48 hours, whatever,

it goes up, the concentration goes up,
then it's cleansed out of your system.
So this is called the concentration curve.

-Hmm.
-You have to match that.

Is that a big science?
When it is released?
Not really. I mean, it's pharmacokinetics.

For a person in the art,
it's not so complicated.
You develop a formulation which is--

is significantly different from a...

because of anything extraneous.

-The product itself is designed to bind.
-Right.

So, the molecule--
It's like you have a lock.
It's a key which goes in and turns.
Right. Does the--

say for example, there is one drug

which should dissolve after,
I don't know, like 30 seconds,
one more after three minutes.
So what changes that?
The way you formulate the product.

The quality of the--
The characteristics of the substance
and the way you formulate it.

-How you make a tablet.
-Right.

How do you make it,

all those things
which help the product dissolve

So you have a tablet you take
and it works for you.

-Right.

I don't think-- That's subjective...

over there are manufactured here.

-Yeah.
-Indian companies.

very stringent when you export to US.

which I know, actually,

when you basically make a drug,
the regulator says

that if the impurities are

For example, you say it is

In India, it's all right.

-No, I wouldn't agree with that.
-No, really?

The standards are the same everywhere.

I think the standard
of Indian regulators' limits

on purities, impurities
are perfectly fine.

In India's side,
you'll always find in tablets

and capsules and medicines,
overage is always there.

That means it is not 100,
it is 100-some milligram.

where the laboratory fails it,
government laboratory fails it.

Like, if something is not sold
for a certain--

I take supplements, okay?

I take everything from magnesium
to sleeping to omega-3 and all of that.

If the bottle is 6 months old
versus fresh, there is a difference?

from a good brand

than rely on a regulatory system
to do this.

But does it deteriorate in terms
of efficacy inside a bottle?

-Every product degrades.
-Right.

Every batch we sell,
we retain a part of it

to study how it's behaving
over the life cycle.
And if there is a problem, we recall it.
Right.
That's a quality system all of us follow.

But any drug you buy anywhere
in the world,
